entry: Mass extinction at the end of the [[Cretaceous]] period, around 65.5 million years ago. It eliminated roughly three-quarters (75%) of plant and animal species on Earth. The non-avian [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]], all [[Pterosaur|pterosaurs]], [[Plesiosaur|plesiosaurs]], mosasaurs, ammonites and rudists died out, as did most other tetrapods weighing more than 25 kg (55 lb), though some ectothermic species such as sea turtles survived. A thin worldwide layer of sediment marks the K–Pg boundary, with unusually high levels of [[Iridium|iridium]], a metal more common in asteroids than in Earth's crust. The leading explanation is an asteroid 10 to 15 km (6 to 9 mi) wide that formed the [[Chicxulub crater]] on the Yucatán Peninsula. Its impact caused a prolonged impact winter that halted [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] in plants and plankton. Mammals diversified in the following [[Paleogene]] Period, and the surviving dinosaurs radiated into modern birds.

Third and last period of the [[Mesozoic|Mesozoic Era]], lasting from about 143.1 to 66 million years ago. At around 77.1 million years, it is the ninth and longest geological period of the [[Phanerozoic]]. Its name derives from the Latin *creta*, meaning [[Chalk|chalk]], which is abundant in deposits from the latter half of the period. The climate was relatively warm, with high sea levels that created numerous shallow inland seas. Dinosaurs continued to dominate the land, and the earliest relatives of placentals and [[Marsupial|marsupials]] appeared, as did the earliest crown group birds toward the end. [[Flowering plant|Flowering plants]] appeared in the Early Cretaceous and became the dominant plants worldwide by the end of the period, as widespread gymnosperm groups declined. The period ended with the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event|Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction]], in which many groups, including non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs and large marine reptiles, died out.

Largest and most populous island of [[Greece]], in the southern [[Aegean Sea]]. Crete lies about 100 km (62 mi) south of the Peloponnese and is the fifth largest island in the [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]], after Sicily, Sardinia, Cyprus and Corsica. It has an area of 8,450 sq km (3,260 sq mi), is predominantly mountainous, and its highest point is Mount Ida. The region of Crete, which includes surrounding islands, had a population of 624,408 as of 2021, with its capital at Heraklion. Crete was the center of Europe's first advanced civilization, the [[Minoan civilization|Minoans]], from 2700 to 1420 BCE. Later rulers included Rome, the Byzantine Empire, the Venetian Republic and the [[Ottoman Empire]]. In 1898 Crete achieved autonomy under the Ottomans, and in December 1913 it became part of Greece. In Greek mythology it is best known as the birthplace of [[Zeus]], and the Minoan palace of [[Knossos]] lies near Heraklion.

Incurable, terminal neurodegenerative disease caused by a [[Prion|prion]]. Early symptoms include memory problems, behavioral changes and poor coordination, and later symptoms include [[Dementia|dementia]], involuntary movements and coma. About 70% of patients die within a year of diagnosis. About 85% of cases occur for unknown reasons, while 10–15% are inherited. A variant form, [[Variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease|variant CJD]], was caused by exposure to meat from cows with bovine spongiform encephalopathy. There is no specific treatment; opioids may relieve pain, and clonazepam may help with involuntary movements.

Quadrennial men's world cup of One Day International (ODI) [[Cricket|cricket]], organized by the International Cricket Council (ICC). It is one of the world's most viewed sporting events. The first tournament was held in England in June 1975, and the first three were all held there. Since 1987 hosting has been shared between countries under an unofficial rotation, with 14 ICC members having hosted at least one match. Australia has won six titles, India and the West Indies two each, and Pakistan, Sri Lanka and England one each. Australia won the 2023 tournament in India. The 2027 edition will be held jointly in [[South Africa]], [[Zimbabwe]] and [[Namibia]], and it will feature an expanded 14-team final competition.

Bat-and-ball team sport between two teams of eleven players on a field. Each end of the 22-yard pitch has a wicket of two bails balanced on three stumps. The batting side scores runs by hitting the bowled ball and running between the wickets, while the fielding side tries to dismiss ten batters to end an innings. Forms range from Test matches of up to five days to Twenty20 (T20), in which each team bats for a single 20-over innings. The sport spread globally with the expansion of the [[British Empire]], and its earliest known definite reference is to play in southeast England in the mid-16th century. The International Cricket Council (ICC) has over 100 members, twelve of them full members who play Test matches. The sport is played mainly in [[India]], [[Pakistan]], Bangladesh, [[Sri Lanka]], [[Australia]], New Zealand, England and Wales, South Africa and the West Indies. Australia has won eight One Day International trophies, including six World Cups.

[[Orthoptera|Orthopteran]] insect of the family Gryllidae, related to bush crickets and, more distantly, to [[Grasshopper|grasshoppers]]. Crickets have cylindrical bodies, long antennae and enlarged hind legs for jumping. Males produce a loud, persistent chirp by rubbing their leathery forewings together, mostly at night. Crickets are distributed worldwide except at latitudes of 55° or higher, with the greatest diversity in the [[Tropics|tropics]]. The largest members of the family are the bull crickets, *Brachytrupes*, up to 5 cm (2 in) long. Crickets appear in literature, including *The Adventures of Pinocchio* and [[Charles Dickens|Charles Dickens]]'s *The Cricket on the Hearth*, and in poems by [[William Wordsworth]] and [[John Keats]]. They are kept as pets in countries from [[China]] to Europe and are eaten deep-fried in Southeast Asia.

Novel by Russian author [[Fyodor Dostoevsky]], serialized in twelve monthly installments in 1866. It was the second of Dostoevsky's full-length novels after his return from ten years of exile in [[Siberia]], and it is considered the first great novel of his mature period. The story follows Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former law student in [[Saint Petersburg]] who plans to kill a pawnbroker. He believes that extraordinary men may justify certain crimes, but after the murder he is overwhelmed by confusion, paranoia and disgust, and his theories lose their power as he faces guilt and consequences. The novel first appeared in *The Russian Messenger*, a prestigious journal that was also the outlet for [[Ivan Turgenev]] and [[Leo Tolstoy]]. It is often cited as one of the greatest works of world literature.

Peninsula in Eastern Europe on the northern coast of the [[Black Sea]]. It is almost entirely surrounded by the Black Sea and the [[Sea of Azov]] and is linked to mainland [[Ukraine]] by the Isthmus of Perekop. Its population is 2.4 million, and its largest city is [[Sevastopol]]. Historically at the boundary between the classical world and the steppe, Crimea came under the Golden Horde, then the [[Crimean Khanate]], a dependency of the [[Ottoman Empire]]. The Russian Empire annexed it in 1783, and its strategic position led to the 1854 [[Crimean War]]. After the Soviets retook the peninsula in 1944, Crimean Tatars were deported under the orders of [[Joseph Stalin]], an act described as cultural genocide. In 1954 it was transferred to the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. Russian forces occupied the peninsula in 2014 and Russia annexed it, but most countries recognize it as Ukrainian territory.

Crimean Tatar state, 1441–1783. Founded by Hacı I Giray, the khanate reached the height of its power in the first half of the 16th century, when it extended from Bessarabia in the west to the North Caucasus in the east. It regarded itself as the heir and legal successor of the [[Golden Horde]]. In the 15th century it became a dependency of the [[Ottoman Empire]]. Lands controlled by Russia and Poland-Lithuania were often the target of slave raids. In 1783, violating the 1774 Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca, the [[Russian Empire]] annexed the khanate, and among the European powers only France protested openly. Its territory centered on [[Crimea|the Crimean peninsula]], and its borders shifted with constant incursions by the [[Cossacks]].

Conflict of 1853–1856 between Russia and an alliance of the [[Ottoman Empire]], France, the United Kingdom and Sardinia. It arose from the decline of the Ottoman Empire and Russian expansion, and from British and French efforts to preserve the Ottomans to maintain the balance of power in Europe. It began with Tsar Nicholas I's demand that the Ottoman Empire's Orthodox subjects be placed under his protection. Britain and France joined in March 1854. Allied forces landed in [[Crimea]] in September 1854 to capture [[Sevastopol]], Russia's main Black Sea naval base, and an 11-month siege followed, with brutal conditions on both sides. The Treaty of Paris, signed March 30, 1856, ended the war and forbade Russia from basing warships in the [[Black Sea]]. The war was among the first to use explosive naval shells, railways and telegraphs. The poor medical conditions it exposed led to demands for professionalized medicine, most famously achieved by [[Florence Nightingale]], who pioneered modern nursing.

Body of law that defines [[Crime|crimes]] and prescribes their punishment. Most criminal law is established by statute and varies by jurisdiction. Unlike civil law, which emphasizes dispute resolution and victim compensation, criminal law includes the punishment and rehabilitation of offenders. Penalties range from fines, probation and house arrest to imprisonment and, in some jurisdictions, [[Capital punishment]] for the most serious crimes. The Code of [[Ur|Ur-Nammu]], written around 2100–2050 BC by the king of Ur, is among the earliest written codes, and the [[Code of Hammurabi]] formed the core of Babylonian law. The state's role in dispensing justice through courts became clear in 18th-century Europe, as countries began maintaining police services.

Interdisciplinary field that studies [[Crime|crime]] and [[Deviance (sociology)|deviant behavior]]. It draws on [[Sociology|sociology]], political science, economics, psychology, philosophy, biology and law, and examines the nature of crime and criminals, the origins of [[Criminal law]], the causes of crime, social reactions to it, and the work of law enforcement agencies and penal institutions. Modern academic criminology has roots in the 19th-century Italian School of "criminal anthropology." The term was most likely coined in 1885 by Italian law professor Raffaele Garofalo. In the United States the discipline grew substantially in the first quarter of the 20th century, and after the 1960s it became institutionalized outside sociology through standalone criminal justice programs.

Rich, deep red color inclining to purple and the national color of [[Nepal]]. It originally meant the color of the dye made from the [[Scale insect|scale insect]] *Kermes vermilio*. Cochineal dyes from the Western Hemisphere replaced kermes in Europe during the [[Columbian exchange]] in the 15th century, as they were more potent. Alizarin crimson, invented in 1868, is a dye bonded onto alum and used as a pigment.

Primarily African-American alliance of [[Gang|street gangs]] based in the coastal regions of [[Southern California]]. Founded in [[Los Angeles]] mainly by Raymond Washington and Stanley Williams, it began as an alliance of two autonomous gangs and developed into a loosely connected network of "sets" that were often engaged in open warfare with one another. Members have traditionally worn blue. With an estimated 30,000 to 35,000 members in 2008, the Crips have been involved in murders, robberies and drug dealing. They have a long and bitter rivalry with the [[Bloods]].

Roman government crisis of 235–284, also called the Military Anarchy. Repeated foreign invasions, civil wars and economic disintegration nearly destroyed the [[Roman Empire]]. Emperor Severus Alexander was assassinated by his own troops in 235, and at least 26 claimants to the title of emperor followed. By 268 the empire had split into three competing states: the Gallic Empire, the Palmyrene Empire under [[Zenobia]], and the Italian-centered Roman Empire proper. Currency debasement and the breakdown of trade and productivity further weakened the economy. Aurelian (270–275) reunited the empire and restored some monetary stability. The crisis is said to have ended when [[Diocletian]] defeated Carinus in 285 and restructured the government, economy and military.

Portuguese football forward, nicknamed CR7. He began his career at Sporting CP and joined Manchester United in 2003, helping the club win three consecutive [[Premier League]] titles and the 2007–08 [[UEFA Champions League|Champions League]]. In 2009 he moved to Real Madrid for a fee of €94 million (£80 million), at the time the most expensive transfer in history, and helped the club win four Champions Leagues and two [[La Liga]] titles. He later played for Juventus and Al-Nassr. His 35 trophies include five UEFA Champions Leagues, two UEFA Nations Leagues and the [[UEFA European Championship]]. He has won five Ballons d'Or and was named the world's best player five times by [[FIFA]]. He holds the men's records for international appearances (234) and goals (146), and in November 2026 he announced his retirement from international football.

End point of a phase equilibrium curve in [[Thermodynamics|thermodynamics]]. The best-known example is the liquid–[[Vapor|vapor]] critical point, the end point of the pressure–temperature curve along which a liquid and its vapor coexist. At this point only one phase exists and the heat of vaporization is zero. Above the critical temperature, a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone. Water's critical point lies at 647.096 K (373.946 °C; 705.103 °F) and 22.064 megapascals. Charles Cagniard de la Tour discovered the liquid–vapor critical point in 1822, and [[Dmitri Mendeleev]] named it in 1860.

Analysis of [[Fact|facts]], evidence and [[Argument|arguments]] to form a judgment. It involves recognizing underlying assumptions, justifying ideas and actions, and assessing their rationality and consequences. Its earliest records are the teachings of [[Socrates]], as recorded by [[Plato]]. The use of the phrase can be traced to [[John Dewey]], who called it reflective thinking. According to philosopher Richard W. Paul, it is a competency that can be learned or trained, requiring self-directed, self-disciplined and self-corrective habits of mind. It presupposes overcoming egocentrism and sociocentrism, which leads to effective communication and problem solving.

Treatise by German philosopher [[Immanuel Kant]], published in 1781 with a second edition in 1787. In it Kant seeks to determine the limits and scope of [[Metaphysics]]. Building on [[John Locke]], [[David Hume]], [[René Descartes]] and [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]], he examines the nature of [[Space]] and argues for transcendental idealism, in which objects are known as appearances rather than things in themselves. His central question is how synthetic a priori judgments, which are informative yet known independently of experience, are possible. The book received little attention at first, but it later shaped [[Western philosophy]] and helped bring about German idealism.

Early modern humans (*Homo sapiens*) who were the first surviving expansion into [[Europe]] and [[Siberia]]. They possibly occupied the continent from as early as 56,800 years ago and interbred with [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]], who went extinct 35,000 to 40,000 years ago. Cro-Magnons were generally more robust than living populations, with larger brains, broader faces and bigger teeth. Their population was much larger than that of the Neanderthals, possibly due to higher fertility rates. They produced [[Upper Paleolithic]] cultures, including the Aurignacian and Gravettian, and an array of art, including [[Cave painting|cave paintings]] and [[Venus (mythology)|Venus figurines]]. The name comes from five skeletons found in 1868 at the Cro-Magnon rock shelter in Les Eyzies, France.

Republic in Central and Southeastern Europe, on the coast of the [[Adriatic Sea]]. Its capital and largest city is [[Zagreb]]. Croatia is a representative democracy with a prime minister, president and unicameral parliament, and it is a member of the [[European Union]], the [[United Nations]] and [[NATO]]. The country covers 56,594 sq km (21,851 sq mi) and has a population of nearly 3.9 million as of 2026. It was a kingdom from 925 under King Tomislav and aligned with the [[Habsburg monarchy]] in 1527, before merging into the Kingdom of [[Yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]] in 1918. It declared independence from Yugoslavia on June 25, 1991, and fought the [[Croatian War of Independence|war of independence]] until 1995. Its high-income economy is dominated by services, industry and agriculture, and tourism is especially prominent.

Armed conflict of 1991–1995 in [[Croatia]] between Croatian forces and the Yugoslav People's Army and local Serb forces. Serb forces established the self-proclaimed Republic of Serbian Krajina within Croatia. Croatia's 1995 offensives, Operation Flash and Operation Storm, effectively ended the war in its favor. Over 20,000 people were killed. In 2015 the [[International Court of Justice]] dismissed mutual claims of genocide by Croatia and Serbia, though it found that crimes against civilians had taken place.

Technique of creating [[Textile|textiles]] by interlocking loops of [[Yarn|yarn]] or thread with a hook. The name comes from the French word *crochet*, meaning hook, and hooks may be made of materials such as aluminum, [[Steel]], wood or bone. Unlike [[Knitting|knitting]], which keeps many stitches open at once, crochet completes each stitch before starting the next, although variants such as Tunisian crochet keep several open. Crocheted fabric first appears in substantial evidence in 19th-century Europe, and the first known published instructions using the term appeared in the Dutch magazine *Penélopé* in 1823.

Large, semiaquatic [[Reptile|reptile]] of the family Crocodylidae, found throughout the tropics in Africa, Asia, the Americas and Australia. Crocodiles tend to congregate in freshwater habitats such as [[River|rivers]], [[Lake|lakes]] and [[Wetland|wetlands]], and sometimes in [[Brackish water]] or saltwater. They are carnivores, feeding mostly on vertebrates such as fish, reptiles, birds and mammals. Unlike alligators, they are very sensitive to cold. Many species are threatened, some critically endangered. The [[Saltwater crocodile]] is the largest, routinely exceeding 5 m in length. Females guard their nests, a rare parental trait among reptiles.
